entry.title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past

media:group.media:title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation: Confronting Our Past
media:group.media:description:
In recognition of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the Office of Indigenous Directions invites the university community to participate in a day of reflection and learning, following the publication of a long-awaited report, Exploring Concordia’s Colonial Past.
Join Manon Tremblay, senior director, Indigenous Directions, and Allan Vicaire, senior advisor, for a conversation about the report and its findings. A discussion will be moderated by Peter Gossage (Distinguished Professor Emeritus, Dept. of History), with the participation of:
Colby Gaudet, the report's author and SSHRC Postdoctoral Fellow in the Department of History at Dalhousie University Kahérakwas Donna Goodleaf, Director, Decolonizing Curriculum and Pedagogy Sigwan Thivierge, Associate Professor, First Peoples Studies & Linguistics Lisa White, Executive Director, Equity Office About the report:
In 2021, Concordia commissioned then doctoral student Colby Gaudet to investigate the university’s historical foundations and produce a report that would help situate the university’s past within the wider context of colonialism and Indigenous experiences.
The research focused on the Grey Nuns, whose former motherhouse is part of Concordia’s campus, the founding institutions of Loyola College and Sir George Williams University and their respective connections to the Jesuits and the YMCA, all of which played roles in broader colonial systems in Canada.
By examining these histories, the report invites the Concordia community to reflect on the university’s past and to support ongoing efforts toward reconciliation and decolonization.
The report will be available for download on September 30th, 2026.

entry.title: Fair Trade at Concordia with Shatha Arslan and Sofia Melatti

media:group.media:title: Fair Trade at Concordia with Shatha Arslan and Sofia Melatti
media:group.media:description: Concordia University is a Fair Trade certified campus; offering a range of Fairtrade product availability for students and faculty while hosting events for engagement. Fairtrade is an ethical certification and sustainability label that puts farmers’ rights at the forefront, ensuring they get paid a fair livable wage. Join us as we present the necessary steps towards gold status campus designation, our outreach with the Concordia community, and our engagement with the academic faculty.

entry.title: Launch of Pathways to Impact with Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox

media:group.media:title: Launch of Pathways to Impact with Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox
media:group.media:description:
Join project team, Prem Sooriyakumar and Brett Cox, to learn more about the launch of Pathways to Impact!
Born from various sustainability lead and focused consultations regarding research impact, Concordia’s Office of the Vice President, Research Innovation and Impact (OVPRII) has launched a new web platform for its Pathways to Impact initiative, an ongoing collaboration with units from across the university designed to help researchers strengthen their research impact.
About the Speakers:
• Prem Sooriyakumar is Tamil, originally arrived as a refugee to Tiohtià:ke, from Jaffna, Sri Lanka. Currently a Senior Knowledge Broker at the OVPRII. He works with researchers on knowledge mobilization planning and research impact development and strategy. Additionally, Prem has been developing and supporting the institutional Pathways to Impact initiative and is one of the senior strategic advisors on the Abundant Intelligences NFRF-T research project, a majority Indigenous lead research project on Artificial Intelligences.
• Brett Cox is a third-generation settler originally from Brantford, Ontario – land that is situated on the traditional territory of the Neutral, Anishnawbe and Haudenosaunee peoples. Since June 2023, Brett has worked as Coordinator of Sustainability in Research at the OVPRII. His work involves coordinating various projects aimed at meeting the goals and strategies of the Sustainability in Research action plan. In addition to any questions related to the Pathways to Impact initiative, you can contact Brett for support with exploring sustainable research practices, developing a research impact plan, and any questions related to Concordia's Sustainability in Research action plan.

entry.title: Indigenizing and Decolonizing Sustainability Curriculum at Concordia

media:group.media:title: Indigenizing and Decolonizing Sustainability Curriculum at Concordia
media:group.media:description:
Join us for the next event as part of the Sustainability Action Plan 2026-30 Launch to celebrate Concordia's new sustainability roadmap.
Learn about the new opportunities and explore ongoing efforts to decolonize sustainability curriculum through partnerships with the Office of Decolonizing Curriculum and Pedagogy, with Donna Goodleaf, Director, Decolonizing and Indigenizing Curriculum and Pedagogy, and Rebecca Tittler, Academic Advisor and Administrative Coordinator at the Loyola College for Diversity and Sustainability and Coordinator of the Loyola Sustainability Research Centre.
About the Speakers:
• Donna Kahérakwas Goodleaf is Turtle Clan and is a citizen from the Kanien’kehá:ka (Mohawk) Nation, Kahnawake Territory, which is part of the Rotinonhsión:ni Six Nations Iroquois Confederacy. She is a Kanien’kehá:ka educator and scholar who joined Concordia university in January of 2018 as the new Indigenous Curriculum and Pedagogical Advisor for the Centre for Teaching and Learning. Her current primary role as Director, Decolonizing and Indigenizing Curriculum and Pedagogy is to develop university-wide training for Concordia faculty on decolonizing and Indigenizing their curriculum programs of study in ways that re-center the advancement and integration of Indigenous peoples’ diverse humanities - intellectual, scientific and cultural knowledge systems, worldviews, epistemologies, histories, research and pedagogies across all academic units. She also serves on Concordia University’s Indigenous Directions Leadership Council.
• Rebecca Tittler is a second-generation settler here in Tiohtiá:ke. She first joined Concordia's Loyola College for Diversity and Sustainability in 2013 as an instructor, adding her current position asAcademic Advisor and Administrative Coordinator at the College and Coordinator of the Loyola Sustainability Research Centre in 2016. In both roles, she has worked and continues to work towards the development of sustainability curriculum that incorporates Indigenous expertise and knowledge systems.

entry.title: The Iron Ring Podcast: What we wish we knew

media:group.media:title: The Iron Ring Podcast: What we wish we knew
media:group.media:description:
Join us for the new episode recording of The Iron Ring Podcast, where WIE hosts Maria Abou Ghazaly, Zineb Bamouh and Allison Shkodra share their experiences navigating engineering at different stages of their academic journeys.
Through the perspective of women navigating a traditionally male-dominated field, the conversation aims to bridge the gap between newer and more experienced engineering students. From academics and internships to finding balance, building connections, and navigating university life, we’ll reflect on what we’ve learned, the challenges we’ve faced, and what we wish we had known when starting out.

entry.title: Ways of Doing Scenography: Light, Memory, and Research-Creation from Valparíso to Montréal

media:group.media:title: Ways of Doing Scenography: Light, Memory, and Research-Creation from Valparíso to Montréal
media:group.media:description:
This public conversation with Tamara Figueroa explores ways of doing scenography through light, memory, territory, and research-creation. Drawing from her practice as a lighting designer, performance designer, and academic from Valparaíso, Chile, the event will address how live arts can produce knowledge, how professional scenic production can generate methodologies for academic research, and how port cities such as Valparaíso and Montréal can open shared imaginaries around movement, memory, ecologies, and ways of inhabiting.
The conversation introduces her current project, Topologías de los sueños, which is in an initial phase and will be developed through the Centro de Investigaciones Artísticas and the Área de Creación at the Escuela de Teatro, Universidad de Valparaíso.
Tamara Figueroa is an academic visitor from Valparaiso in residency in LePARC from September 23rd to September 29th.

entry.title: Life, Edited: Genetic Engineering at Concordia

media:group.media:title: Life, Edited: Genetic Engineering at Concordia
media:group.media:description:
Join us for a panel discussion with Concordia’s iGEM team, where they highlight the potential of synthetic biology to address specific challenges.
You'll hear from experts coming together applying genetic modification technologies and working to decentralize genomics and genetic engineering:
Who leads genetic editing discoveries and innovation? Who is best served by the technologies? And have governance frameworks caught up to the pace of technology so that the public can trust that advancements are responsibly scrutinized?
About the Speakers:
• Austein McLoughlin Programme Mangement Officer at UNEP-SCBD, covering Biosafety and Synthetic Biology.
Austein McLoughlin is a programme management officer at the Secretariat on the Convention on Biological Diversity. He leads on the programmes of work on synthetic biology under the Convention and risk assessment and risk management of living modified organisms under the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. Since 2019, he has been facilitating international discussions on biosafety and synthetic biology, while also supporting capacity-building on these topics in many regions of the world.
• Ben Novak Lead Scientist at Revive and Restore doing genetic rescue of species.
Ben Novak is the lead scientist for the conservation non-profit Revive & Restore. He manages 24 projects developing biobanking, reproductive, and genome editing technologies for amphibians, birds, and mammals, including the audacious effort to recreate the extinct passenger pigeon by the early 2030s. While passenger pigeons are Ben’s passion and specialty, the conceptualization and advocacy of biotech-based genetic rescue solutions for all organisms have been a lifelong pursuit. He leads the world's first genetic rescue cloning programs that produced the first clone of a U.S. endangered species, a black-footed ferret cloned from cells biobanked in 1988. This project represents the first time in history that lost genetic diversity has been restored to an endangered species and is widely recognized as the seminal example of biotechnology's potential value in wildlife conservation.
• Ian Bradbury Research Scientist with the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) and contributor to the federal GenARCC initiative.
Dr. Ian Bradbury is a Research Scientist with Fisheries and Oceans Canada and an Adjunct Professor at Dalhousie University. His research uses genomics to understand how aquatic species respond and adapt to environmental change, with a particular focus on climate change, conservation, and sustainable fisheries. He is Co-Lead of GenARCC (Genomic Adaptation and Resilience to Climate Change), a national research initiative using genomics to understand and predict climate vulnerability and resilience across Canadian species. His work explores the genomic basis of adaptation, population resilience, and human impacts on wild populations, and how emerging genomic technologies can inform conservation and management in a rapidly changing climate.
• Dylan Fraser Professor at Concordia's Department of Biology, focused on ecology, evolution and genetics/genomics for conservation and habitat management.
Dylan's lab integrates ‘eco-evo-gen’ (ecology, evolution and genetics/genomics) towards more effective conservation and management of natural populations, species and ecosystems, with an emphasis on fishes. By bridging these disciplines, we investigate how eco-evo-gen mediates population diversification, productivity, persistence and responses to environmental change, including climate change, fishing and habitat fragmentation.Austein McLoughlin Programme Mangement Officer at UNEP-SCBD, covering Biosafety and Synthetic Biology.
